items.stem: A student’s proposed essay question is: “Why does the government of a low-lying Pacific island state take the view that it demands that high-emitting countries accept responsibility?” What is the main problem with it?
options: It focuses on one perspective, so different perspectives cannot be compared
It is too broad to answer in 2,000 words
It is descriptive, inviting an account rather than an argument
It cannot be researched because no evidence could exist
items.answer: It focuses on one perspective, so different perspectives cannot be compared

items.stem: Arjun proposes this essay question: “Describe the history of the spread of online disinformation during elections.” Identify its weakness and write an improved question, explaining why it is better.
items.answer: Weakness: it is descriptive, inviting an account rather than an argument. Improved: “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?” — focused, contestable and global, so perspectives can be compared within the word limit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark improved question; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: Ines proposes this essay question: “What will the use of economic sanctions be like in the year 2300?” Identify its weakness and write an improved question, explaining why it is better.
items.answer: Weakness: it cannot be researched because no evidence could exist. Improved: “Are economic sanctions an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” — focused, contestable and global, so perspectives can be compared within the word limit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark improved question; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: A teacher is reviewing three essay questions. Question A: “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the education ministry should run citizenship education programmes in schools?” Question B: “Which international body publishes data on low voter turnout among young people?” Question C: “Describe the history of low voter turnout among young people.” (a) Identify the strongest question. (b) Explain how Question A allows the student to compare perspectives.
items.answer: (a) Question A. (b) It is contestable, so e.g. a youth campaign group and a libertarian think tank would answer differently, and their reasoning and evidence can be compared.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark contestable; 1 mark named perspectives; 1 mark comparison [3]

items.stem: Explain why “Are gender quotas the best way to increase the number of women in parliament?” is a suitable question for a Global Perspectives essay.
items.answer: It is contestable, so different perspectives (e.g. UN Women and a party official) can be compared; it is focused enough for the word limit; and it has a global dimension (a world average of roughly a quarter of parliamentary seats held by women, which the Inter-Parliamentary Union tracks, and the UN Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality).
items.markingKey: 1 mark contestable/perspectives; 1 mark focus/feasibility; 1 mark global dimension [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the choice of research question is the most important factor in the success of a Global Perspectives essay.
items.answer: For: A focused, contestable question makes comparison of perspectives possible. A poor question (descriptive, too broad) limits the marks available for analysis and evaluation. Against: The quality of sources and evidence matters as much. Clear structure, evaluation and referencing also determine success. Judgement: The question sets the limits of what is possible, but success depends on research and evaluation too; e.g. “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?” still needs credible sources.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: In an academic database, searching "Security Council" gives 8,100 results and veto gives 9,300; "Security Council" AND veto gives 600. Calculate the number of results for "Security Council" OR veto, and for "Security Council" NOT veto. Explain which search would be most useful for an essay on “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?”.
items.answer: OR: 8,100 + 9,300 − 600 = 16,800. NOT: 8,100 − 600 = 7,500. AND (600) is most useful: it is focused on both aspects and manageable, though still needs filtering by date and source type.
items.markingKey: 1 mark OR with overlap subtracted; 1 mark NOT; 1 mark justified choice; 1 mark further narrowing (filters, date, peer review) [4]

items.stem: Assess the claim that academic databases are more useful than general search engines for researching disputes over shared rivers.
items.answer: For: Databases contain peer-reviewed articles with checked methods. Filters by subject and date give focused, credible results. Against: Academic work may be slow to cover recent events. Search engines find reports by NGOs, international organisations and news needed for current perspectives. Judgement: The best research combines both, evaluating each source’s credibility.

items.stem: In an academic database, searching "economic sanctions" gives 4,200 results and effectiveness gives 2,300; "economic sanctions" AND effectiveness gives 1,200. items.stem: Freya is writing an essay on “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?”. The student reads page 185 of The export of plastic waste to poorer countries: challenges and responses by H. Duarte, published by Harbour Academic Press, London, in 2020. The author writes: “Exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities.” Explain one method of note-making that would help the student avoid accidental plagiarism.
items.answer: Record full source details and page numbers with every note; put copied words in quotation marks and write summaries in their own words, e.g. using Cornell notes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it avoids plagiarism [2]

items.answer: (a) (Duarte, 2018, p. 64) (b) Any accurate rewording keeping the meaning, followed by a citation (Duarte, 2018).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark accurate meaning in own words; 1 mark citation [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that when researching an issue such as state use of facial recognition surveillance, avoiding plagiarism is mainly the responsibility of the student rather than the school.
items.answer: For: Students choose how to take notes and must cite sources accurately. Plagiarism is a matter of academic honesty and personal integrity. Against: Schools must teach referencing and note-making explicitly. Easy access to AI tools and online text means schools need clear rules and checking systems. Judgement: Responsibility is shared, but the student is ultimately accountable for the work submitted.

items.stem: Explain why “To what extent is it the responsibility of the electoral commission to address low voter turnout among young people?” is a suitable question for a Global Perspectives essay.
items.answer: It is contestable, so different perspectives (e.g. a youth campaign group and a libertarian think tank) can be compared; it is focused enough for the word limit; and it has a global dimension (a decline in youth turnout reported across many established democracies, which international bodies such as International IDEA monitor and compare).
items.markingKey: 1 mark contestable/perspectives; 1 mark focus/feasibility; 1 mark global dimension [3]

items.stem: Priya is interested in water, food and agriculture and wants to write an essay. The starting point is the broad topic “Water, food and agriculture”. Write a focused research question on that issue.
items.answer: Should countries upstream on a shared river need the agreement of downstream countries before building dams?
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused; 1 mark contestable [2]

items.stem: Mei proposes this essay question: “What will the spread of online disinformation during elections be like in the year 2300?” Identify its weakness and write an improved question, explaining why it is better.
items.answer: Weakness: it cannot be researched because no evidence could exist. Improved: “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?” — focused, contestable and global, so perspectives can be compared within the word limit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark improved question; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: Ana proposes this essay question: “Describe the history of corruption in public procurement.” Identify its weakness and write an improved question, explaining why it is better.
items.answer: Weakness: it is descriptive, inviting an account rather than an argument. Improved: “To what extent is it the responsibility of the national government to address corruption in public procurement?” — focused, contestable and global, so perspectives can be compared within the word limit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark improved question; 1 mark explains improvement [3]

items.stem: A teacher is reviewing three essay questions. Question A: “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?” Question B: “Why does the African Union (the Ezulwini Consensus) take the view that it demands two permanent seats with veto power for Africa?” Question C: “What are all the causes and effects of every global political and governance issues issue?” (a) Identify the strongest question. (b) Explain the weakness of each of the other questions.
items.answer: (a) Question A. (b) It focuses on one perspective, so different perspectives cannot be compared; it is too broad to answer in 2,000 words.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 2 marks each [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “an online collection of scholarly articles and books, such as JSTOR or Google Scholar”?
options: Lateral reading
Scanning
Boolean operator
Academic database
items.answer: Academic database
items.markingKey: Academic database: an online collection of scholarly articles and books, such as JSTOR or Google Scholar. [1]

items.stem: A student researching lowering the voting age to 16 needs to find a specific statistic in a long report. Explain why scanning is a suitable strategy.
items.answer: Scanning saves time and focuses effort: it lets the student find a specific statistic in a long report without reading every word, so more sources can be considered.
items.markingKey: 1 mark describes the strategy; 1 mark explains why it suits the purpose [2]

items.stem: A student researching threats to press freedom needs to find a specific statistic in a long report. Explain why scanning is a suitable strategy.
items.answer: Scanning saves time and focuses effort: it lets the student find a specific statistic in a long report without reading every word, so more sources can be considered.
items.markingKey: 1 mark describes the strategy; 1 mark explains why it suits the purpose [2]

items.stem: In an academic database, searching "voting age" gives 4,200 results and youth gives 6,700; "voting age" AND youth gives 1,900. How many results would "voting age" OR youth give?
items.markingKey: OR = 4,200 + 6,700 − 1,900 = 9,000 (the overlap is counted once). [1]

items.stem: Ethan is researching the question “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?”. A general web search returns millions of results, including a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties and a leaflet produced by a political party during an election campaign. Suggest a better search string, using Boolean operators.
items.answer: "Security Council" AND (veto OR reform) NOT football
items.markingKey: 1 mark AND/OR combination; 1 mark relevant terms [2]

items.stem: “Academic databases are more useful than general search engines for researching low voter turnout among young people.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Databases contain peer-reviewed articles with checked methods. Filters by subject and date give focused, credible results. Against: Academic work may be slow to cover recent events. Search engines find reports by NGOs, international organisations and news needed for current perspectives. Judgement: The best research combines both, evaluating each source’s credibility.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: “Academic databases are more useful than general search engines for researching migration caused by climate change.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Databases contain peer-reviewed articles with checked methods. Filters by subject and date give focused, credible results. Against: Academic work may be slow to cover recent events. Search engines find reports by NGOs, international organisations and news needed for current perspectives. Judgement: The best research combines both, evaluating each source’s credibility.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: What is meant by “paraphrase” in Global Perspectives?
options: Presenting someone else’s words or ideas as your own without acknowledgement.
The exact words of a source, placed in quotation marks and cited.
Expressing someone else’s idea in your own words, still with a citation.
A short reference in the text, such as (Author, year), linking to the full reference list.
items.answer: Expressing someone else’s idea in your own words, still with a citation.
items.markingKey: Paraphrase: expressing someone else’s idea in your own words, still with a citation. [1]

items.stem: While researching low voter turnout among young people, which action by a student would be plagiarism?
options: Summarising an argument from Petrov in your own words with a citation
Copying a paragraph from a report and changing a few words, without a citation
Including a common-knowledge fact, such as the date the UN was founded, without a citation
Quoting a sentence from Petrov in quotation marks with an in-text citation
items.answer: Copying a paragraph from a report and changing a few words, without a citation
items.markingKey: Plagiarism = using others’ words/ideas without acknowledgement. [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why accurate referencing matters in an essay on migration caused by climate change.
items.answer: It acknowledges others’ work and avoids plagiarism; it lets the reader check the evidence and judge the credibility of sources; it shows the range of research.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: A reference list for an essay on the spread of online disinformation during elections contains sources by: Moreau (2021); Duarte (2023); Chen (2025). In what order should they appear in a Harvard reference list?
items.answer: Chen, Duarte, Moreau.
items.markingKey: Alphabetical by author surname: Chen, Duarte, Moreau. 2 marks fully correct, 1 mark one pair wrong [2]

items.stem: Lina is writing an essay on “Should countries upstream on a shared river need the agreement of downstream countries before building dams?”. The student reads page 142 of Disputes over shared rivers: evidence from ten democracies by E. Novak, published by Meridian University Press, Toronto, in 2018. The author writes: “Shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict.” Paraphrase the quotation in your own words.
items.answer: Any accurate rewording keeping the meaning, followed by a citation (Novak, 2018).
items.markingKey: 1 mark accurate meaning in own words; 1 mark citation [2]

items.stem: Priya argues that when researching an issue such as threats to press freedom, avoiding plagiarism is mainly the responsibility of the student rather than the school. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Students choose how to take notes and must cite sources accurately. Plagiarism is a matter of academic honesty and personal integrity. Against: Schools must teach referencing and note-making explicitly. Easy access to AI tools and online text means schools need clear rules and checking systems. Judgement: Responsibility is shared, but the student is ultimately accountable for the work submitted.
